caseno: Civil Rule No.294 (FM) of 1996. (FMAT No.518 of 1996)
lawyer:
Mainul Hosein with Azizul Haque, Mozammel Huq and Humayun Kabir Bulbul, Advocates — For the Petitioner. 
Rafique-ul-Huq with Md. Sharful Islam Khan and Ahsanul Karim, Advocates — For the Opposite Parties 1 and 3. 
Md. Aminul Hoque with Md. Abdul Jabbar, Advocates — For the Opposite Party No.2.
parties:
PKS Ltd  ----- Petitioner
vs.
IFIC Bank Ltd. and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md. Sirajul Islam J: This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner was issued calling upon the defendant-respondent-opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 to show cause as to why they should not be restrained from Getting refund of the disputed amount of Taka 1,48,00,000/- from the petitioner till disposal of FMAT No. 518 of 1996 pending in this court or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The appellant-petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 117 of 1996 in the court of Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for a declaration that the demand note of the defendant No. 1 issued to the State Bank of India, Overseas Branch Calcutta calling for refund of US Dollar 3,52,000 equivalent to Taka 1,48,00,000 (approx) vide telex No. 01/C/IMPORT/3065/96 dated 20-6-1996 is illegal, inoperative, malafide and not binding on the plaintiff. The plaintiffs case, in short, is that the plaintiff is a reputed company dealing with export of Rice incorporated in India under the Indian Companies Act with its office at the address given in the plaint in Calcutta, India. The defendant No. 2 contacted that plaintiff over telephone on 13/14th December, 1995 requesting him for shipment of 1000 metric tons of rice from India @ US Dollar 235 per Metric Ton. The defendant No. 2 being known to the plaintiff as importer of rice from India since long agreed to the request for export of the said quantity of rice at the aforesaid rate and sent proforma Invoice No. PKS/MT/1073/95-96 dated 16-12-95 and accordingly the importer-defendant No. 2 opened L/C against the said Proforma Invoice vide L/C No. JFJCB/ACU/0001/96 dated 1-1-96 for US Dollar 1,17,500.00 only. After getting confirmation about opening of the L/C by the defendant No. 2, the plaintiff-company made shipment of 1000 Metric Tons of rice by Trucks through Sona Masjid Land Custom Station on Bangladesh border and Mohadipur Land Custom station on the Indian border. After receipt of this consignment of rice the defendant No. 2 through IFIC Bank Ltd. (defendant No.1) requested the plaintiff for sending another consignment of 1000 Metric Tons of rice in the similar way by amending the L/C on 18-1-1996. The plaintiff accordingly sent the consignment through the same route. The defendant No. 2 again requested the plaintiff for sending another consignment of 500 Metric Tons of rice by amending the L/C for 2nd time by Telex dated 6th February, 1996. The plaintiff accordingly sent the same. The defendant No. 2 after receipt of the same again requested the plaintiff for sending another consignment of 1475 Metric Tons of rice by amending the L/C through defendant No. 1 by Telex dated 10-3-1996. In this process the defendant No. 2 received a total consignment 3975 metric tons of rice from the plaintiff to talling the credit value of US Dollar 9,35,125.00. All the above mentioned consignments were sent by the plaintiff after getting clearance from the Indian Customs Authority and the plaintiff company got payment at the first phase US Dollar 4,70,000.00, the value of 2000 Metric Tons of rice. The plaintiff company thereafter received payments of the disputed 1500 metric tons of rice valued at US dollar 3,52,500.00. That the plaintiff being a company of International repute is always diligent about high-rate performance and that after taking the rice tested by Indian Atomic Research Centre, Calcutta properly and correctly, sent the consignments received by defendant No. 2 and payments were accordingly made. Thus after full payment was made the transaction became complete but the defendant No. 1 thereafter raised some objections pointing out some discrepancies like non-receipt of certified invoice from the Sona Masjid Land Custom Station of Bangladesh and on such pleas the defendants 1 and 2 started demanding refund of the price of the disputed rice of 1500 Metric Tons amounting to US Dollar 3,52,000.00 (Taka 1,48,00,000 in Bangladeshi Taka) The defendant No. 2 by an unfair collusion with defendant No. 1 and Bangladesh Custom Authority started demanding the price of last 3 consignments of 500 metric tons each of rice on various illegal pleas through the defendant Bank of the importer. The defendant No. 1, the importer's bank (IFIC Bank) asked its agent, the State Bank of India, Overseas Branch, Calcutta to get refund of money from proforma defendant No. 7, the Union Bank of India and accordingly the defendant No. 1 continued to insist on demanding the refund of money from its agent, the State Bank of India, who in turn is demanding refund from plaintiff's banks United Bank of India. This demand for refund of money already paid to the exporter-plaintiff is illegal and malafide, hence the plaintiff filed the Suit No. 117 of 1996 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for declaration as aforesaid. 

 3. After filing of the suit the plaintiff filed an application under Order 39 rule 1 CPC for temporary injunction restraining the defendant respondent opposite party No. 1 from getting refund of the money. The defendant Nos. 1 and 3 appeared and contested the plaintiff's application for temporary injunction by filing a joint written objection denying the plaintiff's case stating inter alia that the plaintiff received payment of the amount of money of the disputed 1500 metric tons of rice hastily on some illegal and discrepant papers and documents and, as such, the defendants are entitled to get the refund of the money received by illegal means through discrepant papers. After hearing both the parties and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the plaintiff's prayer for temporary injunction vide his judgment and order dated 26-1-96. 

 4. Being aggrieved by this rejection order dated 26-9-1996 the plaintiff as an appellant has preferred FMAT No. 518 of 1996 in this court. After admission of this appeal as FMA the plaintiff appellant PKS Ltd as petitioner has filed a separate application praying for injunction for restraining the defendant respondent-opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 from insisting on getting refund of the disputed amount of money, whereupon the present Rule was issued. 

 5. Only question in this Rule appears to be a question for decision whether the plaintiff appellant petitioner is entitled to get any temporary injunction as prayed for pending disposal of the appeal. 

 6. Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff appellant-petitioner, has submitted that the importer defendant No. 2 duly received the goods sent by the disputed consignments and then being satisfied its bank defendant No. 1 duly made the payment to the seller company through defendants agent bank, State Bank of India at Calcutta, and thus the transaction for payment and receipt with the plaintiff and defendant No. 2 is a completed transaction and, as such, the defendants have no right to demand the refund of the disputed amount already paid to the plaintiff petitioner. Mr. Mainul Hosein further submitted that this is not a case of L/C and so the buyer-defendant No.2 cannot interfere with the payment already made and that it is a bank to bank transaction but that the defendants with a malafide intention started demanding the closed transacted money and, as such, the demand of refund of money already paid is an illegal demand made by defendant No. 1 to the plaintiff and his agent Union Bank of India through defendants Bank State Bank of India and that if the refund is taken by the defendant No. 1 during the pendency of the suit, the plaintiff shall suffer irreparable loss and, as such, the plaintiff is entitled to get a temporary injunction as prayed for. 

 7. Mr. Rafique-Ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 has raised a preliminary objection that the declaration as prayed for by the petitioner is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as the letter of credit is not a property as contemplated in section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that a suit for declaration of title can only be filed by a plaintiff to protect his proprietary right or a legal character but that a letter of credit does not confer any legal right as to property or legal character and, as such, the suit is not maintainable in this form. He further submits that the State Bank of India, the defendant's agent bank is the reimbursing bank but that bank has not been made a party in the suit from whom the demand is allegedly being made by the defendant's issuing bank, IFIC Bank of Bangladesh and in that view of the matter also the plaintiff is not entitled to get any relief of injunction as prayed for. He further submits that defendant No. 1 the IFIC Bank is asking for the refund of the disputed money from its own Bank, the State Bank of India in Calcutta and not from the plaintiff nor from its bank and, as such, the plaintiff's suit itself will not be maintainable as framed and so temporary injunction cannot be granted as prayed for. 

 9. We are primarily to see whether the plaintiff has got any prima facie case for temporary injunction as prayed for. 

 10. The first requirement for the purpose of granting a temporary injunction is to see whether the plaintiff appellant has been able to make out a good prima facie case for getting any temporary injunction. 

 11. In this connection Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Advocate for the defendant opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 referred to Articles 13 and 14A of the ICC Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits, 1993, Revised publication No. 500 (hereinafter referred to as UCPDC) and that L/C is a transaction between bank to bank and that this mechanism of L/C is of different level which must be allowed to be honoured free from interference from any court, otherwise trust in international commerce shall be irreparably damaged and as such the plaintiff is not entitled to get any temporary injunction on an international Trade Transaction between bank to bank. In support of this contention Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq referred to a decision in the case of Tarapore and Co. Madras vs. Tractore Export, Moscow and another reported in AIR 1970 (SC) page 89 wherein it has been held by the Supreme Court of India as under: 

 16. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned advocate submits that the payment was fraudulently obtained by the plaintiff bank on some discrepant papers and that the payment was obtained before verifying the papers submitted to the defendant issuing bank. He submits that defendant's issuing IFIC bank received the documents on 13-4-96 and on the same day the Indian Bank was informed about the discrepancies of the document on 13-4-96 but the bank of India made the payment earlier on 4-4-1996. Mr. Rafique-Ul-Huq referred to Articles 13 (b) of the UCPDC and submits that seven (7) days time is allowed for verification of papers but before this allowable time, payment was made by the Indian bank and therefore, the issuing bank is entitled to get the refund of money as because the payment was made on discrepant papers before verification of the same and in violation of the international principle of payment. Mr. Rafique-ul-Huq drew our attention to a copy of the concerned L/C to show that the documentary credit has been made subject to the Uniform Custom and Practice for documentary credit 1993 Publication No. 500. He referred to a particular condition of the agreement of the L/C wherein it has been stated that the negotiating bank will send a telex to the opening bank at least 3 days prior to the reimbursement claim regarding the payment. Mr. Huq submits that in violation of this condition, the negotiating bank has made the payment on 4-4-1996 only one day after sending the documents on 3-4-1996. 

 17. It appears from the copy of the plaint that the plaintiff has prayed for injunction for restraining the defendant respondent opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 from insisting on getting refund of the disputed amount of money as mentioned in the schedule of the plaint. But it has not been stated from whom the refund of money was demanded by defendant Nos. 1 and 3 and the non-mentioning of the persons or bank from whom the defendant Nos. 1 and 3 will be restrained from demanding money, makes the whole prayer for temporary injunction to be vague, unspecified and unintelligible for the purpose of granting an equitable relief of temporary injunction. 

 18. In this respect Mr. Mainul Hosein, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, submits that this is a new case of this nature and that in spite of some defects in the prayer for temporary injunction, the broad fact remains that the defendant has been insisting on demanding refund from their bank. It is the principle of law that whatever may be the nature of a case, the prayer for an injunction must be made clearly and specifically as to whom to be restrained from making the payment as because the plaintiff must come with clean hand to seek an equitable relief of temporary injunction. There is no such clear or specific prayer in this matter. 

 20. Considering all the above facts and circumstances, we find that the plaintiff has got no prima facie case for any temporary injunction. 

 21. The next question to be decided for the purpose of granting a temporary injunction is whether the plaintiff in the absence of any temporary injunction will suffer irreparable loss. In the instant case we find that the whole case relates to payment or non-payment of money. Plaintiffs case is a case of payment already made and hence the refund of such paid-money cannot be asked for. The defendant's case is that the payment has been illegally obtained by the plaintiff through some discrepant papers in violation of terms of L/C and, international commercial transaction and, as such, the defendant is legally entitled to get back the money. So it appears that the whole subject matter centers round payment and refund of money. If the refund of money is made and subsequently it is found that papers were not discrepant then the question of plaintiff's loss shall arise and that loss will be a money loss which can be safely compensated by paying back money. So the question of irreparable loss is not present in the instant case and, as such, the plaintiff does not appear to have a case for temporary injunction on the ground of irreparable loss. 

 22. The next question is to see whether the balance of convenience and inconvenience lies in favour of the plaintiff for the purpose of getting temporary injunction as prayed for. It has been held by their Lordships in the case of United Commercial Bank vs. Bank of India and others reported in AIR 1981 (SC) 1426 that: 

 "A payment" under reserve" is understood in banking transactions to mean that the recipient of money may not deem it as his own but must be prepared to return it on demand. The balance of convenience clearly lies in allowing the normal banking transactions to go forward. Furthermore, the plaintiffs have failed to establish that they would be put to an irreparable loss unless an interim injunction was granted". 

 23. From the principle as laid down above, it appears that the banking transactions should be allowed to go forward without any hindrance of any sort. Mr. Mainul Hossein submits that the payment in the transaction under consideration in this case was not made under any reserve. But the fact remains that the defendant's clear case is that the payments were made before receipt of papers and documents by the Bank (IFIC) and before getting any opportunity for verification of discrepancies therein. Therefore, the alleged demand has been made by one bank to another bank, making it also a normal banking transaction. Thus it appears that in such case of normal banking transaction the balance of convenience and inconvenience does not lie in favour of the plaintiff for getting any temporary injunction. In the facts and circumstances, we find that balance of convenience and inconvenience for the purpose of equitable relief of temporary injunction heavily lies against the plaintiff. 

 24. In consideration of all the above facts, circumstances and the principles of law, we find that the plaintiff is not entitled to get any temporary injunction in the manner as prayed for. It may be noted here that any of our observations made above will not go to prejudice any of the parties hereof in the disposal of the pending First Miscellaneous Appeal and the suit on merit.
